question.text: Suppose that a $3 \times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: \[ R_2:=R_2-2R_1, \qquad R_3:=R_3-3R_1 \] Given that $C$ has the LU factorization $C=LU,$ then $L=$
question.explanation:
Applying $R_2:=R_2 + ({\color{red}-2}) \cdot R_1$ and then $R_3:=R_3+ ({\color{red}-3}) \cdot R_1$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices: \[ \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0 & 0 \\ 0& 1 & 0 \\ {\color{red}-3}& 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{E_2} \cdot \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0 & 0 \\ {\color{red}-2}& 1 & 0 \\ 0& 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{E_1} \cdot C = U. \]

Now, since $E_2E_1C=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_2 E_1 C &= U \\[1ex] E_1 C &= E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] C &= E_1^{-1} E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] C &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{red}-2} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{red}-3} & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] C &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}2} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}3} & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) U \\[1ex] C &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}2} & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}3} & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \cdot U. \end{align*}

question.text: Suppose that a $3 \times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: \[ R_2:=R_2+9R_1, \qquad R_3:=R_3-2R_1. \] Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
question.explanation:
Applying $R_2:=R_2+{\color{red}9} \cdot R_1$ and then $R_3:=R_3 + ({\color{red}-2}) \cdot R_1$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

\[ \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0 & 0 \\ 0& 1 & 0 \\ \color{red}-2& 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{E_2} \cdot \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0 & 0 \\ \color{red}9& 1 & 0 \\ 0& 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{E_1} \cdot H = U \]

Now, since $E_2E_1H=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_2 E_1 H &= U \\[1ex] E_1 H &= E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] H &= E_1^{-1} E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] H &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \color{red}9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \color{red}-2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] H &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \color{blue}-9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \color{blue}2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) U \\[1ex] H &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \color{blue}-9 & 1 & 0 \\ \color{blue}2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \cdot U \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $ K = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $K=LU,$ then $L=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $K$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $K$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

\[ \begin{align*} K &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + \left(-\dfrac{7}{4}\right)R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\dfrac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot K \\ &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3 \end{bmatrix}& R_3 &:= R_3 + R_2 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_2} \cdot E_1 \cdot K \\[2ex] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_2E_1K=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_2 E_1 K &= U \\[1ex] E_1 K &= E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] K &= E_1^{-1} E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] K &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\dfrac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] K &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \dfrac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) U \\[1ex] K &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \dfrac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 6 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 6 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + \left(\dfrac 1 3\right)R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \dfrac 1 3& 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\ &\sim \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}& R_3 &:= R_3 + R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_2} \cdot E_1 \cdot A \\[2ex] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_2E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_2 E_1 A &= U \\[1ex] E_1 A &= E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= E_1^{-1} E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \dfrac1 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\dfrac1 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) U \\[1ex] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\dfrac1 3 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & -5 & 9 \\ -3 & 0 & -5 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $l_{32}\cdot u_{33}=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & -5 & 9 \\ -3 & 0 & -5 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + \left(-4\right)R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\ &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -3 & 0 & -5 \end{bmatrix}& R_3 &:= R_3 + 3R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_2} \cdot E_1 \cdot A \\[2ex] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -6 & 1 \end{bmatrix}& R_3 &:= R_3 + 2R_2 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_3} \cdot E_2 \cdot E_1 \cdot A \\[2ex] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_3E_2E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_3,$ $E_2,$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_3E_2 E_1 A &= U \\[1ex] E_2E_1 A &= E_3^{-1} U \\[1ex] E_1 A &= E_2^{-1}E_3^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= E_1^{-1} E_2^{-1}E_3^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) U \\[1ex] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

Therefore, $l_{32}=-2,$ $u_{33}=3,$ and $l_{32}\cdot u_{33}=-6.$
